explanation: While the sugar and phosphate group components are identical across all DNA nucleotides, the nitrogenous bases differ. There are four types of nitrogenous bases in DNA: adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C), and thymine (T). Each base has a unique chemical structure, but they are all composed of carbon rings containing nitrogen groups. Based on their ring structure, they are classified into two groups: purines and pyrimidines. Purines are bases with a double-ring structure, which include adenine and guanine. Pyrimidines are bases with a single-ring structure, which include thymine and cytosine.

questions.q: Which of the following nitrogenous bases are classified as purines?
questions.exp: Option C is correct because the slide defines purines as bases with a double-ring structure, specifically Adenine and Guanine. Pyrimidines are single-ring structures, specifically Thymine and Cytosine (Option A). The other options mix purines and pyrimidines.

questions.q: What is the main structural difference between purines and pyrimidines?
opts: Purines have a single ring; pyrimidines have a double ring.
Purines have a double ring; pyrimidines have a single ring.
Purines contain sulfur; pyrimidines contain phosphorus.
Purines lack carbon; pyrimidines lack nitrogen.
